// Each lane is: two-flop synchroniser (the pins are asynchronous to the core

// synchroniser costs two clocks of latency and that latency is CONSTANT,
// which is the whole point: a fixed offset can be calibrated out of a
// FILTW = 0 disables the filter (2-clock latency, 1 clock of uncertainty).

input  wire  logic [NCH-1:0]  fall,      // 0 = capture rising, 1 = falling
input  wire  logic            both,      // capture both edges
output logic [NCH-1:0]        evt_rise,  // polarity of that edge
output logic [NCH-1:0]        level      // filtered live level
for (c = 0; c < NCH; c = c + 1) begin : g_lane

src/sync/sync_compare.sv: // sync_compare.sv — deadline -> trigger pulse, with zero software in the path.
// Arm a channel with an absolute timebase value. When the timebase reaches
// it, the output pin goes high for PW ticks and the channel disarms. The
// output edge lands on the exact clock the deadline is met, so the jitter
// between the programmed time and the pin edge is zero, not "one interrupt
// latency". That is the number that matters when this fires a camera shutter
// The comparison is a signed difference so an armed deadline survives the
// arm: one-hot-ish write of a deadline into channel `sel`
// direct fire, bypassing the deadline compare
for (i = 0; i < NCMP; i = i + 1) begin : g_cmp
// Fire one tick early, because the trigger output is registered:
// that makes the pin edge land on exactly the tick that was
// programmed instead of one after it.
// This looks like it costs a second 32-bit adder per channel, and
// an earlier version rewrote it as `now - deadline >= -1` to avoid
// that. Measured, the rewrite was WORSE: synthesis already shares
// the single `now + 1` incrementer across every channel, while the
// rewrite needs a 32-input AND tree in each one. It cost about
// 1,000 um^2 across three channels. Left as written.
src/sync/sync_event_fifo.sv: // sync_event_fifo.sv — the shared timestamped event queue.
// One queue for all channels rather than one capture register per channel.
// Two reasons, and the second is the important one:
//   area  : eight 32-bit capture registers is 256 flip-flops, which is most
//           of a 1x1 tile. A 2-deep shared queue is 64.
//   order : a shared queue preserves the ORDER of events across channels.
//           Per-channel registers do not, and cross-channel ordering is
//           exactly what you are trying to measure when you sync an inertial
//           measurement unit against an encoder against a camera shutter.
// Entry format (see the README for the bit table):
//   [26:0]  timestamp, low 27 bits of the timebase
input  wire  logic        lost,      // an event dropped before the queue
output logic [31:0]       rdata,     // head, valid while !empty
output logic              overflow   // sticky, cleared only by reset
// a push that finds the queue full is a lost event, and so is
// one dropped on the way in: say so
src/sync/sync_timebase.sv: // sync_timebase.sv — the monotonic clock everything else is measured against.
// This is the part of Tiqora that makes it a clock rather than a counter.

//              resolution is 15.6 ns at 64 MHz and 20 ns at 50 MHz.
//   rate     : a fractional accumulator FRACW bits wide. Each clock it adds
//              |rate|; on overflow the timebase takes an extra tick (rate
//              positive) or skips one (rate negative). With FRACW = 24 the
//              adjustment resolution is 2^-24 tick/clock, about 0.06 parts
//              per million, fine enough to discipline against an external

// clock can make a timestamp go backwards, and every filter downstream of it
// then sees a negative time delta.
// rate discipline: bit 31 is the sign, bits FRACW-1:0 the magnitude

src/tp_pkg.sv: // tp_pkg.sv — shared types and ISA constants for the Tiqora core.
// One package, imported everywhere. ISA constants live here only.
// Xpulse time extension lives in the RISC-V custom-0 encoding space.
localparam logic [2:0] TF3_ARM   = 3'b100;  // TARM   rs1, rs2
localparam logic [2:0] TF3_MARK  = 3'b110;  // TMARK  rd, rs1
localparam logic [2:0] TF3_CTL   = 3'b111;  // TADJ/TRATE/TCFG/TPW by funct7
// Sub-ops carried in funct7 when funct3 == TF3_CTL
localparam logic [6:0] TCTL_ADJ  = 7'd0;    // TADJ  rs1 — step the timebase
localparam logic [6:0] TCTL_RATE = 7'd1;    // TRATE rs1 — fractional rate
localparam logic [6:0] TCTL_CFG  = 7'd2;    // TCFG  rs1 — capture config
localparam logic [6:0] TCTL_PW   = 7'd3;    // TPW   rs1 — trigger pulse width
// These are localparams on plain vectors rather than SystemVerilog
// enums and structs, and that is a synthesis requirement, not a style
// choice. Yosys's native Verilog frontend — which is what the
// Tiny Tapeout hardening flow runs — accepts packages and file-scope
// `import`, but it does NOT accept a typedef'd enum or packed struct
// used as a port or as a variable declaration. A design written that
// way needs the yosys-slang plugin to synthesize at all. Depending on
// a plugin being present in somebody else's continuous integration is
// not a risk worth taking for a tapeout, so the types are spelled out.
// ALU operation, ALU_W bits. Shifts are NOT here: they live in
// tp_shifter so the ALU critical path is one 33-bit adder.
localparam logic [3:0] ALU_COPY_A = 4'd8;   // pass-through for time ops
// tp_decode packs these fields into one CTRL_W-bit vector and
// tp_core unpacks them again. The two concatenations must list the
// fields in the SAME order, which is the order below, most significant
// first. That is one place to get wrong instead of nineteen, and the
// test suite catches a mismatch immediately.
// Sync unit register offsets (word index within 0x2000_0000)
localparam logic [3:0] SR_TIME  = 4'h0;  // R   current timebase
localparam logic [3:0] SR_EVENT = 4'h1;  // R   pop one event (destructive)
localparam logic [3:0] SR_CFG   = 4'h3;  // W   capture enable + edge select
localparam logic [3:0] SR_CMP0  = 4'h4;  // W   compare 0 deadline
localparam logic [3:0] SR_CMP1  = 4'h5;  // W   compare 1 deadline
// offset 6 is deliberately unmapped: the third compare channel is
// reachable through TARM only. Widening the memory-mapped decode was
localparam logic [3:0] SR_PW    = 4'h7;  // W   trigger pulse width
localparam logic [3:0] SR_ADJ   = 4'h8;  // W   step the timebase (signed)
localparam logic [3:0] SR_RATE  = 4'h9;  // W   fractional rate increment
localparam logic [3:0] SR_PULSE = 4'hA;  // W   fire triggers now
// Address map (decoded on addr[31:28] in tp_bus)
localparam logic [3:0] DEV_FLASH = 4'h0;  // 0x0xxx_xxxx external QSPI flash
localparam logic [3:0] DEV_PSRAM = 4'h1;  // 0x1xxx_xxxx external QSPI PSRAM
localparam logic [3:0] DEV_SYNC  = 4'h2;  // 0x2xxx_xxxx sync unit registers
src/tp_sync_soc.sv: // tp_sync_soc.sv — the 1x1 system: sync unit plus a serial host port.
// No core, no external memory, no QSPI. The timestamping and trigger
// hardware is identical to the full chip — same modules, same register
// map, same event format — and a host drives it over the serial port
// instead of a RISC-V core driving it over a bus.
// That is the whole point of the 1x1 build: every claim about timestamp
// resolution, capture latency and trigger jitter holds here too, because
// it is the same logic. What you give up is running a program on the
// chip; the policy loop runs on the host instead.
parameter int PWW   = 16,      // trigger pulse-width counter bits
parameter int DIV   = 434,     // baud = clk_hz / DIV; 115200 at 50 MHz
// head-of-queue exposed for a logic analyser, free of charge
logic [31:0] t_rdata_unused;     // no core to read it
// the Xpulse instruction port is unused without a core
// one-clock pulse whenever the queue gains an entry: the cheapest
// possible scope trigger for measuring pin-to-timestamp latency
// Head-of-queue status on pins. These are already-computed signals,
// so the pins cost wiring and nothing else, and they let a logic
// analyser watch events without the host having to poll.

//   uo_out[4]  TX       serial transmit to the host   (DEDICATED)
//   uo_out[7]  EVTP     one-clock pulse on each captured event
//   uio[4:2]   EVCH     channel of the queued event   (output)
//   uio[5]     EVED     edge of the queued event      (output)
// Serial: 8N1, no flow control, baud = clk_hz / 434, which is 115200 at a

src/uart/tp_host_uart.sv: // tp_host_uart.sv — the host port. This is what makes the 1x1 tile usable.
// Without a core there is nothing on the chip to configure the sync unit or
// read a timestamp back. This module is the missing piece: a serial port
// that reaches the same register interface the bus drives in the full chip.
// "Programmed over USB-C like an ESP32" means exactly what it means for an
// ESP32 devkit: a USB-to-UART bridge presents a serial port on the host and
// drives two pins on the chip. On the Tiny Tapeout demo board that bridge
// is the onboard RP2040, and the pins are the Tiny Tapeout recommended UART
// pins, so no external adapter is needed.
// Wire protocol, least significant byte first throughout:
//   0x01 addr d0 d1 d2 d3   write         0x06                   ACK
//   0x02 addr               read          d0 d1 d2 d3
// `addr` is a sync register offset, 0 to 10 (see tp_pkg.sv). Reading offset
// 1 pops the event queue, exactly as it does from the core in the full chip.
// Area: one 32-bit register carries the write data in and the read data
// out, because the two are never live at the same time. The register port
// is driven combinationally during the single H_DO cycle, so it needs no
localparam logic [2:0] H_CMD   = 3'd0;   // waiting for a command byte
localparam logic [2:0] H_ADDR  = 3'd1;   // waiting for the address
localparam logic [2:0] H_DATA  = 3'd2;   // collecting 4 write bytes
localparam logic [2:0] H_DO    = 3'd3;   // one cycle on the register port
localparam logic [2:0] H_SEND  = 3'd4;   // shifting the reply out
logic [31:0] payload;     // write data in, reply out: never both at once
logic [2:0]  count;       // bytes left to receive or to send
// A byte is launched combinationally, so the transmitter captures
// payload[7:0] in the same cycle the payload shifts down — no separate
// Register port: live only during H_DO, driven straight from state.
// least significant byte arrives first, so shift
// each new byte in at the top
// The access happens combinationally in this cycle; a
// read of tp_pkg::SR_EVENT pops the queue at this clock edge,
// after its head has been captured here.
src/uart/tp_uart_rx.sv: // The bit period is DIV core clocks, so the baud rate tracks whatever
// clock the board runs at: baud = clk_hz / DIV. With the default DIV of
// 434 that is 115,207 baud at 50 MHz, which every serial terminal treats
// as 115200. Run the tile at 25 MHz and you get 57,600 instead — the
// relationship is fixed in silicon and there is no divisor register to
// get wrong, which on a part with no way to recover from a bad setting
// Two flops of synchroniser on the pin, then sample each bit at its
// centre. No parity, one stop bit, no flow control.

output logic             valid     // one clock when a byte has landed
